title: A Bad Spell in the Right Place

pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 9: A bad spell is only a good spell in the wrong place.*

The next week, Dimblewick discovered that dropouts were actually quite handy, provided you did not expect them to follow instructions.

Bunt unclogged the village well by leaning his nose against the stone rim, sniffing deeply at the murky water, and then letting out a sneeze that blasted three hundred years of autumn leaves, a rusted bucket, and one very surprised duckling out of the hole and onto the cobblestones. The Mayor stood in her pink hat, watching the duckling quack indignantly, and decided not to ask questions.

Toby started the town clock. It had been silent for a month, ticking backward in a confused manner. He stood before the great brass face, adjusted his glasses, and shouted, "Stop!" The clock shuddered, let out a long, relieved *tick*, and began to move forward with the confidence of a man who has just remembered his umbrella.

Lulu padded the sagging roof of the bakery with her socks. One hundred and forty-two lavender, polka-dot, and striped socks, packed tight under the shingles. The rain stopped leaking. The baker cried.

Marnie traded her accidental fish for a week of free jam. The cat owner was delighted. Marnie was suspicious.
pages.image: A chaotic village street scene where a large grey-green troll with a mossy hair tuft stands over a stone well, a duckling flying out of the water splashes, while a boy with gold glasses shouts at a large brass clock face and a girl in an orange hoodie packs socks into a roof shingle.

pages.text:
By Friday, the shed had a reputation.

Lulu painted the sign herself. She used purple paint and a troll finger for the letters, because Bunt’s hand was the only thing large enough to hold the brush. "THE DROPOUT CLUB," it read, in wobbly capital letters. Underneath, in smaller script: "ODD JOBS & ODDMENTS (NO SPELLS GUARANTEED)." She apologized to the paint three times. It did not help.

The villagers began to leave gifts. A jar of pickles appeared on the step, smelling of vinegar and hope. A knitted hat, bright red with a yellow pompom, sat on the stove for Gerald. He ate it. He ate it with the dignity of a prince consuming a crown, and then honked at the empty space where his headgear had been.

A blanket, thick and woolly, was draped over the crooked sofa. And then, tucked behind the stove, very small and very old, was a teapot. It was green, with a chip on the spout, and it looked like it had been waiting for this exact shed, for this exact moment, for three hundred years.
pages.image: Lulu stands in front of the plain wooden Potting Shed door with a sock curtain, while Gerald stands beside her and Bunt holds his red-spotted handkerchief.

pages.text:
That night, the stars were out in a way that made the shed look less like a shed and more like a small, crooked star of its own, hanging in the dark.

Marnie sat on the roof, her red sneakers dangling over the edge. Toby climbed up after her, his polished brown shoes squeaking on the shingles with every step. He sat down stiffly, keeping his back straight and his knees together, the way a student sits when the teacher isn't looking.

"I still want one real spell," Marnie said. She did not look at him. She looked at the moon, which seemed very far away and very judgmental. "One that goes the way it should. So no teacher could ever say I can't."

Toby took off his glasses. Without them, he looked younger, and a little softer. He wiped them on his shirt, a gesture so careful it seemed like a ritual, before putting them back on.

"I’d like to light one candle forward," he said quietly. "Just once. Not backward. Just forward. So I could see your face in the flame, not just the dark where the light used to be."

They sat in the silence, listening to the wind move through the leaves, which made a sound like a thousand small, shy whispers.

"We could be wrong about what wrong is," Toby said finally.

Marnie did not answer. She was not ready to believe it. But she did not move away.
pages.image: Two children sitting on the sloping roof of a garden shed under a starry night sky; a girl with copper-red hair buns and a mustard cardigan sits with her legs dangling, and a boy with round gold glasses removed sits stiffly beside her, looking up at the stars with a thoughtful expression.

pages.text:
Gran Pennywhistle arrived with a broom under her arm and a pie in her apron pocket. She did not knock, but simply opened the door, which was propped open with a sock, and walked in as if she owned the place.

She inspected the crooked sofa, poked the sock curtains, and sniffed the air, which smelled of lavender, woodsmoke, and goose.

"In forty years," she said, her voice warm as the pie, "I have mended ten thousand brooms. This is the best-made hideout I have ever seen." She set the pie on the stove, where it was still warm.

Marnie looked up. "Gran, why does that broom wobble?"

Gran smiled, the kind that had seen a lot of wobbles and loved them all.

"The best broom is always the one with the little wobble," she said. "It’s the only one that dances." She patted Marnie’s head. "A stiff broom just drags. A wobbly broom flies."
pages.image: An elderly woman with a grey bun and lavender apron standing in a cozy, cluttered garden shed, smiling warmly as she pats the head of a young girl with copper-red hair, while Gerald watches them from the floor near a pot-bellied stove.

pages.text:
The night before Founders’ Day, the shed settled into a quiet hum while the socks were folded and the stove was banked, leaving Gerald asleep with his purple ribbon tucked neatly under his wing.

A piece of paper slid under the door without a rustle, lying there smooth and gold-edged like a slice of expensive butter.

Marnie picked it up to find handwriting that was spidery and precise, the kind of scrawl that looks like it was done by a spider who had been to finishing school.

"Humbleton Academy cordially invites the Dropout Club to the Founders’ Day Ceremony, in the interest of public relations."

They read it three times, with Bunt’s nose twitching while Lulu stopped fidgeting with her braid ribbon and Toby straightened his bow tie, his hands trembling just a little.

"He means he wants us where he can see us," Toby said.

Lulu stood up and smoothed her orange hoodie, looking at the pile of socks before turning to the door.

"I’ll wear my good socks," she said.
pages.image: Four children gathered around a small wooden table in a dimly lit shed, looking down at a piece of gold-edged paper; a girl in an orange hoodie stands with her hands on her hips looking determined, a boy with gold glasses holds the paper, and a large troll leans in to read, while Gerald watches from the background.
